digest.top_line: PACE-B 5yr PROMs: pad-free 91% SBRT vs 90% CRT, bowel and erectile outcomes comparable — no late PRO penalty for 5-fraction prostate SBRT.
digest.tldr: Prostate carried the day's only signal: PACE-B's 5yr patient-reported outcomes show 5-fraction SBRT tracking conventionally fractionated RT on continence (91% vs 90% pad-free), sexual function and bowel domain. Source reports raw proportions only, with no between-arm estimates and denominators falling from ~400 to ~250, so read as reassurance rather than formal non-inferiority.

sites.intro: Late toxicity, not efficacy: the question is whether ultrahypofractionation costs anything in patient-reported GU, GI or sexual function at 5yr.

verdict.rationale: Prespecified-population PROM readout from a completed phase 3 RCT; supports SBRT as already-adopted practice rather than changing it. No between-arm inferential testing in source.

studies.significance: The 5yr continence numbers are the transferable part: pad-free 91% (233/257) SBRT vs 90% (225/250) CRT, with leak-free 64% vs 69%, so five-fraction SBRT carries no late urinary penalty at the horizon where late RT toxicity usually declares itself. This supports offering SBRT as the default fractionation rather than reserving it.
studies.monday_clinic: In localised prostate cancer already committed to definitive external-beam RT, this supports SBRT over conventional fractionation on 5yr patient-reported urinary, bowel and sexual outcomes; it does not compare RT with prostatectomy or active surveillance.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Patient-reported outcome analysis of the **phase 3, international PACE-B** randomised trial, comparing **SBRT vs conventionally fractionated radiotherapy**. PROMs collected **baseline to 5 yr** and presented as waffle charts for visual alignment with surgical series.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Men with **localised prostate cancer** randomised in PACE-B. Baseline PROM denominators were **367-415 per arm**, falling to **238-265** at 5 yr.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Patient-reported **urinary continence** (leak-free, pad-free, leakage bother), **sexual function** (intercourse-adequate erections, sexual bother) and **bowel** domains (bowel bother, stool incontinence). No oncological endpoint is reported here.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Urinary continence at 5 yr was **comparable**: pad-free **91% (233/257) SBRT vs 90% (225/250) CRT**, leak-free **64% vs 69%**. Bowel bother was low in both arms (**5% each at 5 yr**).

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents men with localised prostate cancer selected for definitive external-beam radiotherapy on a phase 3 protocol. Does not represent men managed with prostatectomy, brachytherapy, or those requiring androgen deprivation or nodal treatment, whose PROM trajectories differ.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The source explicitly frames these data against **TrueNTH 1-yr robotic prostatectomy PROMs**, using a shared waffle format. That is a presentational alignment between two separate cohorts at different timepoints, not a randomised RT-vs-surgery comparison, and the continence contrast it invites should be read as such.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The abstract reports **proportions only**: no confidence intervals, no between-arm test, and no adjustment for the roughly **one-third drop in respondents** from baseline to 5 yr. Whether non-responders differ systematically by arm is not addressed, and PROM completion is rarely missing at random after RT.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The reading is that late patient-reported morbidity does not diverge between five-fraction and conventional schedules out to 5 yr, closing the main remaining objection to SBRT adoption. It does not settle how these numbers compare against surgery, which the waffle-chart framing invites but the design cannot answer.

studies.interpretation:
The clinical question this readout closes is narrow and worth stating precisely. PACE-B's oncological non-inferiority was never the live objection to five-fraction prostate SBRT; the objection was late toxicity, on the reasonable prior that a large dose per fraction should be less forgiving to the urethra, bladder neck and rectal wall over a horizon longer than the two or three years most trials report. Late RT morbidity declares itself slowly, and a schedule that looks clean at 2 yr can separate later. Five-year patient-reported data is therefore the relevant test, and it does not separate: pad-free 91% (233/257) with SBRT against 90% (225/250) with conventional fractionation, bowel bother 5% in each arm. That is the result that matters, and its value lies in the timepoint rather than the effect size.

How much should this move a reader's confidence? Two features argue for taking it seriously. The comparison is randomised, so the arms should be balanced on the baseline continence and erectile function that dominate these endpoints, and the baseline figures reported here are indeed close between arms. And the endpoint is the patient's own report, which is the right instrument for a question about bother rather than about a clinician-graded event. Two features argue for restraint. The abstract gives proportions with no interval and no between-arm test, so a reader cannot bound how large a real difference these data exclude; with roughly 250 evaluable men per arm the confidence bounds around a 1-point difference in pad-free rates are wide enough to accommodate a clinically visible gap. More importantly, respondents fall from close to 400 per arm at baseline to around 240 to 265 at 5 yr. PROM attrition after prostate radiotherapy is not plausibly random with respect to symptoms, and the direction of that bias is not stated. If the arms shed respondents differently, the apparent equivalence is softer than it reads.

The leak-free figures deserve their own note, because they run in the opposite direction to the pad-free ones: 64% with SBRT against 69% with CRT, while pad use is identical. The consistent reading is that SBRT is associated with slightly more men reporting any leak while producing no difference in leak severe enough to need a pad. That is a distinction with real consultation value, and it is the kind of gradient that a single composite continence endpoint would have hidden.

The surgical framing needs care. Presenting these data in the same waffle format as TrueNTH robotic prostatectomy PROMs makes a cross-cohort comparison visually available, and the format will invite it. But PACE-B randomised RT against RT, not against surgery, and the men in a surgical series differ in age, comorbidity and stage in ways that no amount of shared visual grammar corrects. The honest use of the alignment is to make radiotherapy PROMs legible to a reader accustomed to surgical ones, not to license a continence comparison the design cannot support.

For practice, the decision this moves is fractionation, and it moves it toward five fractions as the default for men already committed to external-beam treatment rather than a schedule reserved for the convenience-limited. What would have to be true for that to be wrong is that the 5 yr non-responders carry the toxicity, differentially in the SBRT arm. That is testable against completion rates by arm and by baseline symptom score, and it is what a reader should look for in the full report.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Pad-free 91% (233/257) SBRT vs 90% (225/250) CRT at 5yr, with bowel bother 5% in both arms, is the late-toxicity horizon that mattered for five-fraction adoption. Leak-free was 64% vs 69%, a mild any-leak gradient without a pad-use difference, worth naming in consent.

papers.title: Patient-reported Outcomes After Prostate Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy at 5 yr: Results from the PACE-B Trial.
papers.abstract: Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) complement oncological endpoints by capturing what matters most to patients. The TrueNTH surgical collaboration presented 1-yr PROMs following robotic prostatectomy using accessible visual formats. We present 5-yr PROMs from the phase 3, international PACE-B trial, which randomised men with localised prostate cancer to stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or conventionally fractionated radiotherapy (CRT). PROMs are reported from baseline to 5 yr and presented using waffle charts to enable visual alignment with surgical outcomes. At 5 yr, urinary incontinence outcomes were favourable and comparable between SBRT and CRT. Leak-free rates were 64% (164/258) for SBRT and 69% (172/249) for CRT, pad-free rates were 91% (233/257) for SBRT and 90% (225/250) for CRT, and moderate or big urinary leakage problems were reported by only 6% (15/250) for SBRT and 4% (9/244) for CRT. Intercourse-adequate erections declined in both groups from baseline to 5 yr: from 35% (133/374) to 17% (43/250) for SBRT, and from 40% (157/391) to 20% (47/240) for CRT. Moderate or big sexual problems increased in both groups, from 24% (87/367) to 31% (74/242) for SBRT and from 22% (85/382) to 32% (77/238) for CRT. Bowel effects were low and comparable between groups, with moderate or big bowel problems reported by 2% (7/397) at baseline and 5% (12/265) for SBRT at 5 yr, and 2% (9/415) at baseline and 5% (13/253) for CRT at 5 yr. Stool incontinence as a moderate or big problem rose from <1% (1/374) to 2% (4/240) in the SBRT group and from <1% (1/395) to 3% (7/238) in the CRT group.
